takeaways: The headline number missed: adjusted net income of $2.07 a share vs roughly $2.21-2.22 expected.
But fee-related earnings, the steady management-fee profit investors pay up for, rose 23% to $802 million ($1.28 a share) and beat estimates (Seeking Alpha).
On a GAAP basis Apollo swung to a net loss on investment-related losses (Dow Jones), the volatile part of the business tied to its Athene insurance arm and marks on investments.
Growth engines kept running: record origination of $114 billion in the quarter, $270 billion of inflows over 12 months, and assets under management hit about $1.07 trillion.
CEO Marc Rowan said core earnings power is "poised for a robust close to 2026 with a strong setup for 2027." The dividend stays at $0.5625.
verdict: Apollo missed the headline and the stock went up anyway, because investors only really pay for the fee machine, and the fee machine beat. Wall Street: where losing money on investments is fine as long as you charge enough to manage them.
